The window is open and the curtain breathes. Not quite a wind, just the room adjusting to being alive, a slow exhale of fabric against the frame. I have been thinking about water lately, specifically the sound it makes when it leaves a faucet, that particular sigh before it hits porcelain, before it becomes something you can wash with, something you can drink, something you can use to dilute the day’s confusion. There is a theology in plumbing if you listen closely enough, and I have listened. I have watched the steam rise from my cup like a small prayer being corrected by the atmosphere, rising, thinning, disappearing into the grammar of the room where it is not needed.

A thousand words is an arbitrary number, but then again so is a day, so is a heartbeat counted in isolation, so is the distance between here and wherever you thought you were going. I could tell you about my childhood bedroom, the blue wallpaper that peeled at the corners like old sunburn, the way I used to press my ear against the heating vent and hear the house talking to itself, pipes knocking in a language older than English, older than the building, perhaps older than the idea of shelter. But that was then, and now is now, and now I am here, in this chair, with a pen that leaks ink if you hold it too long, which is a kind of honesty I appreciate in objects that refuse to perform perfection.

What do people want when they ask you to write whatever comes to you? Usually they are not asking for a product. They are asking for permission to stop performing, for a brief suspension of the self-censor with its tired metaphors and its insistence that everything must mean something immediately. I am trying to honor that request. Here is a memory that arrived without invitation, without the courtesy of a knock: a woman on a train platform, carrying a bouquet of daisies wrapped in yesterday’s newspaper, and the way she looked at the tracks as if they were the only honest thing in the world, straight lines that do not pretend to be anything else, that do not curve to please anyone. I have held that image for years, not because it is beautiful, though it is, but because it resembles a feeling I have not yet named.

I have collected small things over time. A button that fell from a stranger’s coat in the rain, a forgotten button that now lives in my drawer like a specimen. A ticket stub from a cinema that burned down years ago, the fire itself a kind of editing, removing what did not serve the narrative. The smell of old paper, which is not unlike the smell of time passing, which is not unlike the smell of rain that has forgotten why it fell, that has become only its own physicality, its own wetness. I keep them in a drawer that sticks, which makes opening it feel like an event, a small ceremony of retrieval, a ritual acknowledgment that the past is not dead but merely stored in imperfect conditions.

There is a theory that the brain stores memories not as photographs but as feelings first, images second, narratives third if you are lucky and if the feeling was strong enough to demand a story. I believe this. I do not remember the exact shade of my first bicycle, whether it was red or blue or that particular green that looks like moss, but I remember the freedom of its metal against my knees, the sound of the chain when I pedaled too fast, the particular tilt of the universe when you realize you have been moving away from home without anyone’s permission, without anyone’s even noticing that absence is a kind of presence.

The coffee is cold now. I do not mind. Cold coffee tastes like decisions made, like the moment after a long conversation when you realize you have said something true by accident, that your mouth has moved faster than your caution. I have done that, spoken truths I did not intend, and later wondered if honesty is just a form of clumsiness, if we are all only dropping our notes in the street for others to find, if the mess we make is the message we send whether we plan it or not.

Time moves differently when you are not measuring it, when you stop checking the clock and instead check the light, which is a more reliable clock anyway. I have watched ants cross the entire width of a kitchen floor and felt a kinship with their seriousness, their refusal to hurry, their understanding that the world is large and they are small and both conditions are adequate, even beautiful. I have been small and I have been large, mostly in my own imagination, which is a country I visit frequently, one with poor infrastructure but excellent scenery, a place where the roads are made of what you wished you had said.

What if I told you that I am writing this not because I have something to say but because the alternative is silence, and silence is too heavy for this particular afternoon, too dense, too full of echoes? The light is shifting now, the window has become a rectangle of gold where dust motes dance in a choreography that predates human observation, that does not require an audience. They are not dancing for me. They are simply existing, and in their existence they remind me that I do not need to justify the time I spend here, that presence is enough, that being is not a debt owed to productivity.

I have passed the middle of this word count, I think, though the number is no longer real; it is just a horizon, and I am walking toward it not because I must arrive but because the walking is the point. I could stop here, in this sentence, and declare victory, but victory seems like the wrong word for this kind of work. It is not conquest. It is weather. It is the slow turning of air in a room that has been closed too long. It is the recognition that you do not need to earn the right to occupy a page.

I will mention one last thing, though I do not know if it is last: the feeling of finishing something you did not plan to begin. It is like opening a door you thought was a wall. Behind it is not a room but a different quality of attention, a softer focus, the recognition that the ordinary is not a failure of imagination but its true source, the ground from which everything else grows. The cup, the curtain, the distant train, the cold coffee, the ink that leaks, the dust that moves: they are enough. They have always been enough. I am writing this to prove it, and in proving it I am only showing you what was already true, which is that you do not need to ask permission to fill a space with your own weather.

If this is a thousand words, then it is also nothing, which is to say it is exactly what it needs to be. I leave you with the sound of the faucet, with the window open, with the curtain still breathing, and with the understanding that whatever came to me today was enough, was always enough, is enough now.
